options.name: P2MR
options.gloss: Pay to Merkle Root (BIP-360): the scriptPubKey commits to a Merkle root of leaf scripts, so no EC point is on chain before a spend

options.name: P2TRv2
options.gloss: Pay to Taproot v2: BIP-341 semantics plus PQC leaf types, an EC point on every output, ECC key path expected to be disabled later

options.name: P2TRH
options.gloss: Pay to Taproot Hash: like P2TRv2 but the scriptPubKey is a hash of the tweaked key and the key path uses public key recovery

options.name: P2QR
options.gloss: Pay to Quantum Resistant: the P2MR structure with all ECC opcodes disabled from the start

options.name: P2TRv2 plus CISA
options.gloss: P2TRv2 bundled with cross input signature aggregation as a single deployment

options.name: CISA output type
options.gloss: A standalone aggregation output type (BIP 460) deployed separately from the PQC work

options.name: Tripwire
options.gloss: An on chain proof of an ECDLP break automatically disables ECC spends inside the output type

options.name: Miner Lockdown
options.gloss: A hashrate majority trigger that disables ECC spends inside the output type

options.name: New witness style
options.gloss: An extra witness with its own discount and costing rules, needing a serialization and P2P change

options.name: Public Key Recovery
options.gloss: Spending without publishing the public key, saving about 32 bytes at the cost of a BIP-340 variant and of batch validation

options.name: Hybrid PQC opcodes
options.gloss: Opcodes that accept an ECC and a PQC signature together

options.name: Separate PQC leaf version
options.gloss: PQC opcodes confined to a leaf version that has no ECC opcodes

options.name: Upgrade hook
options.gloss: A dated anyone can spend deadline that forces a later consensus patch

options.name: CISA
options.gloss: Cross input signature aggregation itself, argued as a bundle or as a later separate step

options.name: SNARK signature aggregation
options.gloss: Post mine SNARK aggregation of signatures to curtail chain growth

options.name: SHRINCS
options.gloss: A hash based signature proposal not coupled to a block size increase

options.name: Half aggregation flow
options.gloss: Who aggregates signatures and where, signer side or relay side

options.name: Later CISA opt in flag
options.gloss: A pubkey grind bit or an extra output byte that lets a later CISA fork reuse the same witness version

options.name: Two stage deployment
options.gloss: A simple first output type now and a fuller one later

options.name: Extension block
options.gloss: A separate block area with its own UTXO set

options.name: Replay protection
options.gloss: Opt in replay protection shipped with the first SegWit v2

claims.quote: This loses some spending efficiency compared to P2TR (see below), but does not reveal EC points on chain before spending.
Leaves an EC point exposed on chain for every output, but is most similar to today’s usage.
The exact same semantics as BIP-341 P2TR, but with PQC opcodes/leaf types added
Key path spending uses public key recovery (see below), giving it the same weight profile as P2TRv2, without EC point on chain.
Needs a new BIP-340 variant, and breaks batch validation.
This makes it unconditionally quantum-resistant, but loses the efficiency of ECC even before Q-day.
This reduces the spending size by ~32 bytes by not publishing the public key explicitly at spend time
at the cost of needing a BIP-340 variant, and breaking batch validation.
This comes at the cost of needing to deploy a transaction serialization change and P2P protocol extension.
This makes it unambiguously clear that EC disabling is expected.
This avoids the need for ecosystem action for EC disabling, at the cost of giving miners more power.
This provides security if a PQC scheme were broken (possibility classically) or used incorrectly
The downside is (even) larger signatures and higher verification costs.
at the cost of preventing the usage of (user-defined) hybrid schemes in script.
P2TRv2 preserves the same fee profile as P2TR, avoiding “not migrating because it costs more”
For developers/infrastructure, it is maximally close to today’s world, avoids the complexity of adding a new witness style or a new ECC signature scheme.
It is compatible with most/all workflows I’m familiar with, including xpub/descriptor sharing
No P2MR or P2TRH. These add additional complexity, cost, or both, to users that may stifle adoption
the additional security to be had from the ability to not expose EC points on chain before ECC spending requires careful and uncommon workflows from users anyway
The actual automatic ECC-disabling mechanisms (especially Miner Lockdown) that may be more bikeshed-prone could be introduced later
To prepare for longer-term full migration, a P2MR-based output type, with Tripwire and Miner Lockdown as well, plus a new witness style
No more P2TR variants, to avoid the overhead/complexity of a privileged ECC-only path which is useless in a post-ECC world.
given that PKR verification is (slightly) slower than normal ECC verification, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to just use normal BIP-340 for ECC instead
P2TRv2 is effectively offering users the ability to opt out of making that call themselves.
P2QR would only be adopted by a tiny minority
Even a few weeks notice may be enough with Miner Lockdown.
The P2MR witness comes out 32 bytes lighter than the equivalent P2TR script path spend at every depth
a P2TR key path spend at 64 witness bytes stays far cheaper, consistent with the 64 vs 128 comparison in the table.
Of the types listed, P2MR (and P2QR, which shares its structure) is the only one that is nearly free to implement given taproot
P2TRH and PKR need a BIP-340 variant, and the new witness styles need serialization and P2P changes.
CISA provides a natural vessel for P2TRv2 which is asymptotically (as the number of outputs inputs grows) so efficient as to only require 1 byte witnesses for full-agg EC spends.
CISA’s output type requires we post bare EC pubkeys on-chain in the SPK and so it has the same PQ-security profile as P2TRv2.
P2MR can also be deployed with CISA, but we cannot use public-key recovery (except for with one input, according to @starius)
This trick works for P2TRH as well, with asymptotic EC witness weight reduced to 32 bytes per input (just one pubkey per full-agg output).
P2TRv2+CISA will be so overwhelmingly efficient compared to P2MR (with or without CISA), that I expect most users will gravitate towards P2TRv2
With CISA, disabling ECC and switching to PQC is now even more expensive than it would’ve been without CISA.
we’ll still want P2MR (possibly deployed without any ECC?) for maximum efficiency after Q-day.
maybe SNARK aggregation could be the silver bullet to incentivize migration to PQ.
users may not want to adopt things that increase cost. This is why I argued against (pure) P2MR before.
adding CISA to the mix may be a net negative for the goal of getting the long tail to adopt PQC
I even have a mild concern about entities taking a stance of “we’ll do a big rewrite one day and switch from P2TR to P2TRv2+PQC+CISA, but stick with P2TR for now”
I wouldn’t do this for the intermediary-step P2TRv2 output type, but if the differentiation becomes that P2MR is more for the longer term, it does make sense to have it there
Or, it may even be reasonable to assign it a cost that’s similar to CISA, without actually needing aggregation of the signatures.
I am very skeptical about the idea of having aggregation be done incrementally by third-party relay nodes
I would caution about thinking of anything as a silver bullet; most if not all things come with significant trade-offs.
they could still very easily deploy the CISA output type using non-aggregated BIP340 signatures for spending.
Currently i gravitate away from the idea, even for P2MR.
A block size increase of the magnitude needed to make even the smallest (XMSS) hash-based sigs fee-competitive with ECC would be an 8 fold increase
to increase the block size, we must also allow retroactive aggregation of signatures (or blocks) via SNARKs to curtail chain growth
With SHRINCS we have not coupled our proposal to a blocksize increase - at least, not initially.
in the near-term it seems like SNARKs will remain far too large to be practical within bitcoin transactions.
adding CISA to the P2TRv2 bundle will increase the time it takes for P2TRv2 to become available, and that will likely reduce adoption before Q-day by the long tail more than fee incentives will
Post-Q-day, if hash-based PQC is adopted, I think the need for a different witness costing rule (and thus larger (pre-aggregated) serialized block sizes) is almost an inevitability
Of all the potential ways additional block data impacts network properties, I consider archive node storage size the least concerning.
Aggregation, even at the block level, won’t remove the need for bandwidth for transaction relay prior to block building.
I agree, it shouldn’t. I think in general the “near-term P2TRv2” idea shouldn’t include any such thing in general.
To give a different weight to block data (below 1 WU/byte) you need a new witness extension
If we bundle CISA+P2TRv2 then P2TRv2 can’t deploy until CISA consensus validation rules are ready. Perhaps you’re right.
However I do think you underestimate the mass appeal of an output type with PQC support which is also the cheapest output type available.
Heck, people seem to like P2MR quite a bit even though until very recently it was twice as expensive as P2TR.
if compute cost is a more important metric, and a witness extension with a new steeper discount is acceptable, then SHRINCS can be parameterized to target a low computational cost per byte
as far as I am concerned they are complete with reference implementations and pretty extensive test vectors.
What this should do is take wallet adoption out of the equation since there is no need for them to adopt any new signing logic.
This also goes for the design details of the necessary companion pieces: tripwire, miner lockdown etc.
CISA can be an insurance to keep driving adoption in this scenario when CRQCs may be closer than they appear.
Realistically, I don’t think we should expect CISA to have a bigger impact than that, I think.
That sounds more like an argument that people like P2MR for other reasons than its economics.
An extension block, as discussed years ago as a scalability proposal, is something very different and much more invasive than what we’re talking about here.
I am just talking about a new witness in transaction serialization, like Segwit did
I feel like P2TRv2 and CISA kind of pull in opposite directions in terms of messaging.
So I don’t think you can draw any meaningful conclusions: prior to this year, getting cheaper fees was an open research problem
I think for exchanges it could be significant – maybe reducing tx fees by 30% for larger consolidation txs
8MB blocks with w=64 seems almost appealing (pq sigs ending up 2.77x as expensive as a schnorr sig, while being 5.5x the size of a schnorr sig
I’d argue for a general tx weight limit (which would implicitly limit serialized size up to style=1).
I tend to agree with Pieter that it’s somehow slightly ‘off’ to merge CISA into this.
CISA, I agree, does not have nearly as big of a selling point in practice as some people want to believe.
The best CISA can hope for is that a 20-25% discount for consolidation matters, I think.
This is why I think bundling would help PQC adoption in many possible scenarios.
Having a P2TRv2 with PQC and another P2TRv3 with CISA seems to be worse for adoption in my mind.
P2TRv2 + PQC + CISA could be implemented and used without CISA (only use plain BIP341 opted-out) or without PQC
I do see the P2TRv2 with an ulterior disablement of ECC spends within the output type itself as a reasonable path forward.
This avoids any kind of generic freezing debate.
About the idea bundling P2TRv2 with CISA, I would rather suggest a no.
i’m +1 with a flexible no-special witness no CISA version of P2TR2 and a latter P2MR based output with a new witness structure and consensus accounting optimization of the whole.
Quantum-resistance is the greater selling point, which is why i think P2MR is still the best option on the table.
if your goal is to maximize migration for the “long-tail” of retail wallets who don’t care about PQ, then it seems like P2TRv2+CISA is the best choice for you
Without CISA, we might as well do P2MR.
Also note that P2TRv2 by itself does not address the critical security risk (ECDLP being broken).
We’ve been talking about P2TRv2 as if it will be an easy upgrade that even lazy wallet devs can manage, or at least that it’s easier than supporting P2MR.
Simply “bumping the witness version” is insufficient even for P2TRv2, with or without CISA.
Where I can be skeptical, it’s on the wallet and node complexity changes required to support CISA in itself.
So yes with this information in mind, a *naked* P2TRv2 sounds less interesting.
it does sounds to me technically possible to introduce discount for a future post-quantum scheme by introducing a novel witness scheme at the same time.
the part where it’s unclear and where I’m a bit skeptical is on the half-aggregastion and full aggregation flow.
My main view is simply that CISA won’t help adoption, and is thus not worth the additional complexity of consensus changes.
Neither P2TRv2 nor P2MR are a “quantum secure output type” in an absolute sense.
I believe that it is a practical impossibility for many software and users to adopt workflows in which P2MR provides quantum-resistance, due to ingrained use of public key sharing.
Having a separate, and possibly later-dated, separate P2QR or P2MR output type (with new witness styles etc) can fill that need.
I like the idea of a two-staged approach, with the first stage being as simple and uncontroversial as possible.
I think there should be at least one in the initial deployment, to set a clear expectation.
A tripwire is probably the best choice.
Finally I’d like to suggest we consider replay protection, from the start.
we could allocate 1 bit of the public key to mark it anyone-can-spend, with the later CISA fork using that as the opt-in all wallets set it by default
Neither helps with the anonymity set , and moving forward such a flag would likely reveal wallet capability.
It’s about why the first output type (the P2TRv2 one) does not use P2MR or P2TRH.
No. If it needs to cover key path spends (which is the most interesting application), it needs a separate output type.
That makes it, for all intents and purposes, a separate output type. Just one that shares the same witness version.
Either at the expense of making every output 1 byte larger, or extra complexity due to having to grind an extra bit. Neither is hugely appealing.
i wasn’t suggesting naked P2TRv2 - I think that’s a bad idea, because it’d be unsafe to use due to the risk of later confiscation via tripwire.
I was pointing out that P2TRv2 is not actually quantum-secure unless key-spending is disabled punctually later.
P2TRv2 is easy to use “correctly” but even with correct usage your coins are not necessarily safe. With P2MR, perfectly “correct” usage is harder, but has meaningful impact on security.
With CISA in play, i feel like we can accept that insecurity as a trade-off in exchange for the better classical performance
Because they’re two radically different proposals with radically different motivations, that’s all I meant.
They might be orthogonal elements of a proposal on paper, but might not be in practice.
That is a significant change for no conceivable benefit.
This is prevented with the explicit opt-out rules for these signatures which works well with a potential second reason that motivated adoption of the output type, like the PQC stuff discussed here.
Yes, it’s possible. But most users won’t, and not recognizing that is not responsible design.
If you view P2TRv2 as insufficiently secure, why would you want anyone to use it, and worse, incentivize it with CISA?
I don’t consider that acceptable. You’re proposing an output type that, barring a future consensus change, automatically becomes insecure.
I want to remove friction that may stand in the way of adoption. Fee increases may be one of them.
i agree with Pieter that P2TRv2 and CISA pull in opposite directions.
I believe Tripwire without miner lockdown is a non-binding constraint and as such does not really provide “teeth” to EC disabling
Miner Lockdown, while it gives the collective of miners the ability to (i believe irrationally) trigger it prematurely, may help in reassuring those stakeholders
I think risk mitigation (P2TRv2 + Tripwire) and full migration (P2MR + eventual EC disabling + Witness style) should be provided in separate deployments.
Crucially, address reuse is not a problem for properly managed long-term holding addresses, simply because address reuse per se does not cause funds to have an exposed public key
P2TR and P2TRv2 are both clearly a regression from a PQ perspective compared to P2WPKH and other address types with hashed keys, until/unless ECC spending is disabled.
moving such funds to P2MR rather than P2TRv2 would certainly feel less risky to someone who is informed about the potential threat of a CRQC.
If people believe they are too risky, P2TRv2 likely won’t reach consensus in the first place, with or without CISA.
which is part of the reason for favoring also adding a later-stage P2MR output type in addition to the long-tail P2TRv2 one
If CISA truly does make P2TRv2 more appealing (which I’m skeptical of), that shouldn’t be a reason to let it compromise on your sense of security about it.
That’s fair. But I also don’t think these are the target audience for P2TRv2. If they’re properly managed they can migrate in time to a later P2MR output type too.
My stance is still that P2MR is the only truly post-quantum address format.
I believe that the benefits of P2TRv2 compared to P2MR (drop-in compat, 8vb efficiency gain) are negligible compared to the existential risk of all the P2TRv2 coins being exposed on Q-day.
An upgrade hook’s deadline is fixed, certain, can be deferred at will, and requires no migration (provided the upgrade is completed or deferred in time).
I’m still partial to P2MR (and/or CISA) + tripwire with a rudimentary hash-based PQC spending path as the first stage.
I personally agree, and think we should treat and identical, because their difference only matters under a tenuous condition (no address reuse/pubkey sharing)
aha, i stand corrected!
All a wallet has to do to support CISA key-spending (opt-out path) now is to bump their witness version.
In the taproot upgrade, a significant amount of additional cryptographic design and implementation complexity was devoted to removing just a single byte from every key and signature
in retrospect I agree the complexity of saving that one byte was probably not worth it.
Then at least we can correctly claim we have deployed a quantum secure output type, and shame wallets who don’t migrate.
Actually it is possible to deploy P2TRv2 with a time-based upgrade hook that transmutes P2TRv2 outputs into anyone-can-spend after a specific deadline block height T
I don’t think CRQC-skeptic CISA enthusiasts would accept an expectation that their EC spending path becomes unspendable before CRQCs materialize.

questions.text: Should the first PQC opcode be hybrid, accepting an ECC and a PQC signature together, despite the extra adoption complexity?
Do we want P2TRv2 plus CISA as an intermediate stage in the migration path, or should CISA stay out of it?
Does the fee efficiency of an output type only matter once it becomes less efficient than what exists today?
Which tip synchronization metrics matter most when signatures get larger: block propagation, transaction relay, or validation cost?
Would the review work needed to land CISA draw reviewers away from the post quantum side and delay it?
Why is merging CISA into the PQC output type work considered off?
Who performs CISA aggregation in practice: wallets alone, full nodes, or mempool logic that does not exist yet?
Was the first P2MR in the two stage plan a typo, or did it mean not in the same deployment?
Can a v2 SegWit be designed so CISA soft forks into it later without another witness version bump?
Would those against CISA today accept a time based upgrade hook so it can be activated on P2TRv2 later?
Why include the orange threat model at all, given that under its assumptions today's hashed key outputs would already be secure?
Is CISA being pictured without PQC support, or without a tripwire?
